posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md:
Gabor did--he used the mercury green line.

But besides Gabor, has anyone reading this ever try such a thing? I mean, you'd think that just by using a mercury lamp and some interference filters stacked one on top of another (three of them), you can get the necessary monochromicity required for the interference fringes.

If you tried it, how did your gram turn out? I mean could you even get a grating out of it? Did you ever get a desired 3-D effect (regardless of how crude it may have been)?

posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md: The earliest holos of Leath & Upatnieks, plus those of Denisyuk, were recorded using the Hg lamp. The only contemporary holographer that I have ever heard mentioning doing this was Rich Rallison, who claimed to have made holos in the dark of night using a street light. But then again...

posts.author: zipsister
posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md:
Way back in the mid 1980's while doing my Masters I took a cement paver, inner tube and holo plates and set up the lot on a street corner in the middle of the night and made some crude laser-like in-line transmission holograms (subject of of my degree work; 'In-Line Holography as an Art Technique') using street lighting. I was careful to pick a corner where there was no multiple interference from more than one light. For an object I used clear persex with scratched images on one surface placed up against the hologram emulsion. Then the police pulled over and questioned me about what I was doing loitering around street corners in the dead of night with a cement paver on top of a floaty. I got as far as "...the coherence of Sodium street lights creates crude interference between..." before they were back in their patrol car and half way back to the station.

zipsister

posts.topic_title: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.author: walschuler
posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md: As I mentioned in a post to the Lippmann part of this site earlier tonight, I did some images using a sodium safe lamp, and a reflective mylar film in fair contact with a holographic emulsion. I estimate the coherence length was in the neighborhood of a millimeter. I got clearly 3-D images of the hills, valleys and dimples in the mylar, created by my imperfect handling of the film and its imperfect contact with the emulsion.

posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md:
> **walschuler:** As I mentioned in a post to the Lippmann part of this site earlier tonight, I did some images using a sodium safe lamp, and a reflective mylar film in fair contact with a holographic emulsion. I estimate the coherence length was in the neighborhood of a millimeter. I got clearly 3-D images of the hills, valleys and dimples in the mylar, created by my imperfect handling of the film and its imperfect contact with the emulsion.

If you have got as much as 1 mm. coherence length then you did well!

I am curious to know what you mean by a “sodium safe lamp”.

Does this mean that it operates at a lower pressure than a sodium street lamp I wonder? ( The higher the pressure in sodium and mercury lamps the broader the emission lines and the worse the potential coherence length).

Years ago I also tried that street experiment with my recording plate resting on polished copper coins under a sodium lamp.

I could only get the metallic rim effect of the coins showing up well and none of the embossed patterning or lettering except a little bit of the queen’s cheekbone. So I reckon my street lamp’s CL was worse than 100microns or 0.1mm.

Jeff

posts.author: Martin
posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md:
> **jeff-blyth:** I am curious to know what you mean by a “sodium safe lamp”.

I guess he meant a low pressure sodium vapor lamp - the kind that used to serve as safelight for panchromatic photographic materials.

These lamps have two strong and very narrow lines close to 589nm – see [http://www.lambdasci.com/download%20pdf/LLE-2.pdf](http://www.lambdasci.com/download%20pdf/LLE-2.pdf)

However, these lamps are not particularly good at making a point light.

posts.author: walschuler
posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md: Yes, it was a low pressure sodium vapor lamp, used in my school's darkrooms as a safelight. I have the specs somewhere, but I think it was about 150 watts. Eventually I bought my own tube and built a diffuser box and used it first to create a field of pure color, just aiming at the diffuser, and then used it to illuminate objects in a darkened room. I photographed using a 4x5 Speed Graphic with old plate holders or film holders. All this was in aid of my Lippmann research.

posts.post_subject: Holography minus the laser--anyone try this?
posts.content_md: With a green sensitive photopolymer more than 40um thick, I've got a transmission image of a tungsten filament (the image is not sharp, but has some deep location) when the film is wrapped around the lamp and exposed for few seconds, seems that CL for that is 1 - 2 um and the filament is recorded in transmission mode similar to circular stereograms, I'm curious and would like to make a "street holography" with a bypass mirror soon, I wonder what is the power street measure since I could not wrap the film onto lamp...
